definition: A thin disc of ultra-pure silicon, 300 mm across for leading-edge chips, on which hundreds of identical dies are printed and later cut apart. Foundries price their output per processed wafer.

The printing step of chipmaking: a scanner projects light through a patterned mask onto a light-sensitive coating on the wafer, defining one layer of the circuit. A modern chip needs dozens of such layers.

A quartz plate carrying the pattern of one circuit layer, used as a stencil in lithography. A full set for a leading-edge chip costs millions of dollars, one reason chip designs are expensive to change.

Extreme-ultraviolet lithography: printing with 13.5 nm light so the finest layers can be exposed in one pass instead of several. EUV scanners are made only by ASML; High-NA EUV is the next generation, with a field half the size of today's.

The next generation of EUV scanners with a larger numerical aperture (0.55) for finer features. Its anamorphic optics halve the maximum exposure field to about 429 mm², which pushes large chips toward multi-die designs.

A generation of chip-manufacturing technology (e.g. TSMC N7, N4, N3, N2, A16). The names are marketing labels rather than physical dimensions; each new node packs more transistors per area at a higher price per wafer.
A transistor design in which the gate surrounds stacked silicon nanosheets on all sides, cutting leakage versus the older FinFET. TSMC's N2 is its first GAA node.

Routing a chip's power wires underneath the transistors instead of through the signal layers above them, freeing space and reducing voltage loss. TSMC calls its version Super Power Rail and introduces it with the A16 node.
A company that manufactures chips designed by others (TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, SMIC). NVIDIA, AMD, Google and Qualcomm are 'fabless': they design chips and buy wafers from foundries.
How many complete dies fit on one wafer, a geometry calculation that depends on die area and the partial dies lost at the round wafer edge. Roughly 63 for an 814 mm² GPU die on a 300 mm wafer.
The average number of random killer defects per square centimetre of wafer, the key quality metric of a fab process. Yield falls roughly exponentially with die area times defect density.
The share of dies on a wafer that work. Big dies have lower yields because each one is more likely to contain a defect, which makes large GPUs disproportionately expensive.

Selling dies that contain a defect by disabling the faulty block (for example a few streaming multiprocessors) and shipping the part as a slightly smaller configuration. It raises the effective yield of large GPUs.
A smaller die designed to be combined with others in one package, instead of building one huge monolithic die. Chiplets improve yield and let different functions use different process nodes.
A very short, very wide link between dies in the same package that lets them act as one chip. NVIDIA's Blackwell uses a 10 TB/s link (NV-HBI) between its two compute dies.
A die (or HBM stack) that has been fully tested before packaging. Because a finished package cannot be reworked, testing each part first avoids scrapping expensive good parts with a bad one.

A thin layer of silicon (or silicon bridges in an organic layer) on which GPU dies and HBM stacks sit side by side, carrying tens of thousands of fine wires between them. It is what makes HBM's terabytes-per-second bandwidth possible.

Techniques that join several dies and memory stacks in one package with far denser wiring than a circuit board, such as TSMC's CoWoS (2.5D) and SoIC (3D stacking). For AI accelerators it has become a capacity bottleneck and a major cost item.
Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test: companies such as ASE and Amkor that package and test chips for fabless designers and foundries.
Original design manufacturer: contract manufacturers (Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron and others) that design and build servers, trays and racks to a customer's or NVIDIA's reference design.
The list and cost of every component that goes into a product. For a GPU package: logic dies, HBM, packaging, substrate and test. Analyst estimates put a B200's at roughly $6,400.
